terms.tip: The short code a stock trades under, like NVDA for Nvidia or RY.TO for Royal Bank on the Toronto exchange.
A price history rewritten so stock splits and dividends don't show up as fake jumps or drops.
A chart scale where equal distances mean equal percentage changes, so a double from $10 to $20 looks the same as from $100 to $200.
A fund that trades like a single stock but holds a basket of investments, such as all 500 stocks in the S&P 500.
A list of stocks used to measure a market, like the S&P 500 (500 big US companies) or the TSX 60.
What the whole company is worth on the stock market: share price times number of shares.
A very small public company, roughly under $300 million in value. Prices swing wildly and trading costs are high.
The highest and lowest closing prices over the past year.
A fund that removes the effect of exchange-rate moves, so you get the stock's move without the currency's.
The average closing price over the last set number of days, recalculated every day. It smooths out the noise to show the trend.
A moving average where every day counts equally: add up the last n closes and divide by n.
A moving average that gives recent days more weight, so it reacts faster than a simple average.
When a faster moving average moves above or below a slower one, often used as a buy or sell signal.
Golden cross: the 50-day average moves above the 200-day. Death cross: it moves below. Widely watched, but slow.
An uptrend is a run of higher highs and higher lows, usually with price above a rising moving average. A downtrend is the reverse.
Support is a price level where falls tend to stop; resistance is a level where rises tend to stall.
Owning things while they're rising and getting out once they start falling, rather than trying to predict turns.
The tendency of assets that have been rising to keep rising for a while, and falling ones to keep falling.
A bull market is a long stretch of rising prices; a bear market is a fall of 20% or more from the peak.
Stan Weinstein's idea that stocks cycle through four stages; Stage 2 is the advancing stage, with price above a rising 30-week average.
A fixed set of instructions that says when to own something and when not to, written down so anyone can test it.
When a rule buys, then sells soon after at a lower price, because the trend it saw wasn't real. Choppy markets cause lots of them.
Moving in and out of the market based on a forecast or rule, instead of staying invested.
Running a rule on past prices to see how it would have done. Useful, but the past never repeats exactly.
Buying and never selling. Every rule on Quiplee is compared against simply holding the same stock.
What you compare a strategy against. On Quiplee it's buy-and-hold on the same stock.
The average yearly growth rate, compounded. 10% a year for 20 years turns $10,000 into about $67,000.
The whole gain or loss over the full period, including dividends. +300% means $10,000 became $40,000.
How far an investment fell from its highest point before recovering. A −50% drawdown means half the value was lost at the worst moment.
How much the price swings around, measured as the yearly standard deviation of returns. Higher means a bumpier ride.
Return earned per unit of risk taken: the return above cash, divided by volatility. Higher is better; the S&P 500 runs around 0.5.
Return judged against how much risk it took to get it, usually by the Sharpe ratio.
The share of a rule's finished calls that turned out right. Trend rules often win under half their calls and still come out ahead.
How often the rule changes its call. More switches means more trading costs, more tax events and more whipsaws.
The share of days the rule was holding the stock rather than sitting in cash.
What it costs to buy or sell: commissions plus the gap between buying and selling prices.
One hundredth of a percent. 5 basis points = 0.05%.
Short-term US government IOUs, treated as 'cash'. When a rule is OUT, Quiplee assumes the money earns the T-bill rate.
In-sample is the data a rule was designed on; out-of-sample is new data it never saw. Only out-of-sample results are a fair test.
Tuning a rule so closely to past data that it captures noise, then fails on new data.
Testing only on stocks that survived to today, which makes every strategy look better than it really was.
Keeping most of your money in a long-term 'core' and applying a rule only to a smaller 'satellite' slice.
Deciding how much money goes into each holding, so no single position can do too much damage.
Bringing a portfolio back to its target mix by trimming what grew and adding to what shrank.
Spreading money across many investments so one bad outcome can't sink the whole portfolio.
Using borrowed money (or debt inside a company) to magnify results. Gains get bigger, and so do losses.
Betting on a price falling by selling borrowed shares and buying them back later. Losses are unlimited if the price rises.
Tax-Free Savings Account (Canada): gains and withdrawals are tax-free, so switching in and out triggers no tax.
Registered Retirement Savings Plan (Canada): contributions are tax-deductible and growth is tax-deferred until withdrawal.
Profit from selling an investment for more than you paid. In a regular (non-registered) account, part of it is taxable.
Canadian tax rule: if you sell at a loss and buy the same stock back within 30 days, you can't claim the loss yet.
Cash a company pays out to shareholders, usually every quarter.
The desk's judgement of whether a news story is likely to change how much money the company brings in.
A company's own forecast of its future sales or profits. Changes to guidance often move a stock more than the actual results.
When a company reports profits below what analysts expected.
On the desk: the share of a source's directional calls that matched the stock's actual next-day move.
The desk's grouping of companies by how they tend to behave under stress, such as 'fortress mega-cap' or 'leveraged cyclical'.
The rough range of losses similar companies took in past crashes. Historical and approximate, not a forecast.
When a company issues new shares, shrinking each existing shareholder's slice of the company.
How easily you can buy or sell without moving the price. Big stocks are liquid; tiny ones often aren't.
